transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-04-30 09:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Liam Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Rao (Redwood SE), Marcus Lee (Redwood Product); Nina Patel (AstraHealth CTO), Roberto Gomez (Head of ML), Sasha Ivanov (Security Lead)

Summary (auto): Edge-cases demo covering long-context streaming + high TPS; focused Q&A on timeouts and private deployment.

00:00 Liam Chen: Alright hi everyone, thanks for joining, this is Liam from Redwood, i'll kick us off. We have Priya our SE and Marcus from product. Nina, Roberto, Sasha, thanks for making time.
00:18 Nina Patel: Thanks Liam. We wanted to see how Redwood behaves when we push really long contexts and also our peak workloads — we do like 1k sustained qps on some endpoints during reports.
00:30 Liam Chen: Great, that's exactly what we planned. Quick agenda: API behavior with long contexts, demo in Console of observability, then Optimize suggestions for batching/caching, and finally Q&A on security and deployment options.
00:45 Priya Rao: I'll start with the API. So re: long context — Redwood supports streaming of tokens for models that can handle long context. For our compiled runtime we have KV cache optimizations and checkpointing to reduce re-compute.
01:05 Roberto Gomez: Sorry, when you say KV cache, is that per-request or shared across requests? How do you handle invalidation with PII?
01:14 Priya Rao: Good question. It's per-model-shard KV cache, not a customer-shared global. For PII we recommend prefix-level cache control — you can opt out of prefix caching on a per-route basis. For Private deployments you can also control persistence.
01:32 Sasha Ivanov: Is the persistence encrypted with customer KMS? We need key separation.
01:36 Marcus Lee: Yes, for Private and Dedicated we integrate with customer KMS/HSM for at-rest encryption of cache snapshots and logs. In hosted we use our KMS but we provide strong audit logs.
01:50 Nina Patel: Can you show the Console when there's backpressure?
01:54 Priya Rao: Yep — switching to the Console. (screen share) So here's the per-route dashboard; top left shows token-level latency, token throughput, errors. If we hit backpressure you'll see a spike in queued requests and an increase in streaming reconnects.
02:20 Liam Chen: I'll simulate a long context stream now — Priya will start a 100k token session and we'll push sustained TPS.
02:30 Priya Rao: Starting the streaming demo. Note: transcription may lag on the screen share — but backend logs are live.
02:50 [02:50] Speaker 2: (background) so the stream starts, you can see the KV hits increasing...
03:10 Priya Rao: We're at ~200 tokens per second aggregated and KV hit rate is 85%. Latency is stable at 220ms token generation on the gpus we have for this demo.
03:28 Roberto Gomez: Wait 220ms per token at 200 tps sounds high — i.e. what is your end-to-end latency per request at our 1k qps target?
03:38 Priya Rao: Right — per-token isn't directly translatable to per-request. For avg request that returns 50 tokens you'd see ~11s if serialized — but with batching and streaming you can reduce client-observed latency. For high QPS we use continuous batching and route by latency SLO to cheaper variants for lower priority traffic.
04:05 Nina Patel: Our priority is tail latency — can't have >2s 95th for some endpoints.
04:13 Marcus Lee: For that we recommend Dedicated capacity pinned to a tier that meets your 95th. We also offer autoscale policies with headroom to avoid queuing.
04:30 Sasha Ivanov: On streaming backpressure — what's the client behavior if the server drops connection or times out? We had connectors that failed silently.
04:40 Priya Rao: Good callout. Our SDKs implement automatic reconnect with resume using the KV cache and continuation tokens; if a stream disconnects the client can re-open and pick up near the last token. Timeouts are configurable client- and server-side.
04:58 Roberto Gomez: Does resume re-run tokens or do you rely on KV to avoid re-computation?
05:04 Priya Rao: We rehydrate via KV so re-computation is minimal. There's a small tail recompute window but it's usually a few tokens.
05:18 Nina Patel: Can you show logs for a simulated timeout?
05:22 Priya Rao: Yep — switching to logs view. Here we have a timeout at 05:12, you can see the stream reconnect events, the resumed offsets, and a metric 'stream_resume_success_rate'.
05:42 Liam Chen: For customers doing PHI workloads you often want Private deployment. Nina — is your procurement leaning Private or Dedicated?
05:52 Nina Patel: Likely Private. Our compliance requires full VPC peering and customer KMS, and we want the control plane on our side for audit.
06:02 Marcus Lee: Private supports customer-managed control plane and on-prem packaging. We also provide RBAC, SAML SSO integrations, and long-term audit retention as an add-on.
06:18 Sasha Ivanov: Any independent certifications?
06:21 Marcus Lee: We are SOC 2 Type II compliant for our hosted control plane and have an ongoing roadmap for ISO certifications. For Private deployments we provide artifacts and support for your audits.
06:34 Roberto Gomez: Back to performance — can we push to 1k tps during the demo?
06:38 Priya Rao: We can simulate burst but not sustain full-provisioned QPS on demo infra. However we have a benchmark harness — I can run a load test in our staging cluster and share the raw traces.
06:50 Liam Chen: We'll do that as a follow-up item — Priya will run a full throughput benchmark with your sample workload.
07:00 Priya Rao: Switching to Optimize. Redwood Optimize suggests batching parameters, cache TTLs, and quantization profiles based on your workload. For long-context we often recommend 8-bit quantization with preserved attention kernels to keep perf while saving memory.
07:18 Roberto Gomez: How do you validate quality after quantization? We can't regress clinical summaries.
07:24 Priya Rao: We run evals against your prompt set and have quality monitors tied to thresholds; Optimize will flag regressions and can rollback to higher-precision variants automatically.
07:38 Nina Patel: Important — our legal will need traceability: prompt/response logs, who accessed them. Is that included?
07:46 Marcus Lee: Yes audit logs track access and API keys. In Private you can forward logs to your SIEM and integrate with your KMS for key access policies.
08:00 [08:00] Speaker 3: (murmur) can we see the per-token cost delta with quantization?
08:05 Priya Rao: Here in the console Optimize panel shows estimated cost per 1M tokens with and without quantization, and expected latency delta. For a lot of customers quantization reduces cost 30-50% with <2% quality impact on evals.
08:20 Roberto Gomez: That's promising. Our runbooks can't tolerate silent quality regression though.
08:25 Priya Rao: Understood — Optimize integrates with canary rollouts and auto-fallback so you can A/B and automatically revert on regression.
08:40 Nina Patel: Can you describe failure modes for streaming under memory pressure? We saw timeouts when the model exceeded memory and processes OOMed.
08:50 Priya Rao: On GPU OOMs we have per-inference isolation, and runtime will fall back to a smaller variant or CPU path if configured. There's a setting for graceful degradation: rather than hard fail, we can return a truncated result with a metadata code so app-level logic can re-request or call a simpler model.
09:10 Sasha Ivanov: Are those responses traceable to a cause in the logs?
09:13 Priya Rao: Yes — error codes, memory utilization, and fallback decisions are logged per-request in the trace.
09:25 Roberto Gomez: What about network backpressure between our VPC and your private control plane? Any best practices?
09:32 Marcus Lee: For Private we recommend using regional peering and dedicated networking with QoS rules. We also support ingress rate limits and client-side buffering to smooth bursts.
09:45 Nina Patel: If we do a POC, can you run it in our AWS account?
09:50 Liam Chen: Yes we can do a private deployment POC where we deploy a sandbox in customer VPC with limited support access. That's typically how we validate tail latency and security controls.
10:02 [10:02] Speaker 1: (interruption) question on SDKs — do you provide automatic resume for web-sockets and SSE?
10:08 Priya Rao: Yes SDKs for Node/Python have built-in reconnect/resume logic for websockets and SSE streams. There's also a raw HTTP API for serverless integrations.
10:20 Roberto Gomez: Any examples of reconciling token offsets between client and server? We had off-by-one issues previously.
10:28 Priya Rao: We emit a resume token representing the last confirmed token id; clients checkpoint that id locally. On reconnect client sends resume_id and server starts dispatching from the next token. Off-by-one typically comes from buffering at client side.
10:44 Nina Patel: Ok let's talk procurement pain points — lead times, contract terms.
10:48 Liam Chen: For Dedicated capacity we have monthly and annual commits; POC pilots often convert to a 6–12 month ramp. We'll share SOW and standard MSA. Dedicated pricing will be in the doc i send.
10:59 Sasha Ivanov: For Private, how invasive is the control plane install?
11:03 Marcus Lee: We have an installer that runs in your VPC; it requires certain outbound endpoints for license checks and telemetry unless you opt for air-gapped mode where we exchange signed artifacts. Our solutions engineering team will map that to your security requirements.
11:20 Roberto Gomez: One more question — if we have a long context session that spans many requests, how do you bill? Per token always, or is there session pricing?
11:29 Priya Rao: We bill per token for generation and a per-embedding unit for embeddings. For long sessions tokens are still the metric. We do offer committed throughput pricing to help with cost predictability.
11:40 Nina Patel: Are there rate limiting and quotas per API key? We may segregate by tenant.
11:44 Liam Chen: Yes per-route and per-api-key limits, and you can implement hierarchical quotas via the Console.
11:52 [11:52] Speaker 2: (crosstalk) what's the expected time to get the benchmark results back?
11:55 Priya Rao: I can run the benchmark in staging and share raw traces in 48–72 hours depending on run complexity.
12:05 Nina Patel: Good. We're concerned about streaming timeouts during peak traffic windows; can we set shorter server timeouts but keep client reconnect aggressive?
12:14 Priya Rao: Absolutely — timeout policies are configurable. Also if you use our SDKs, reconnection is managed automatically and we surface metrics in Console so you can tune.
12:28 Roberto Gomez: Any gotchas with prefix caching when some prompts include PHI?
12:33 Marcus Lee: Don't cache prefixes that include PHI — mark those routes as no-cache. For Private deployments you can also encrypt cache snapshots with your KMS and set TTLs to zero.
12:45 Nina Patel: Ok let's wrap. Any final notes?
12:49 Liam Chen: Quick recap: we'll run a 100k-token streaming benchmark and a sustained throughput test; share Dedicated and Private pricing/SOW; provide Console docs and Optimize recommendations; schedule SE deep-dive for streaming backpressure.
13:04 Priya Rao: Action items recorded — I'll start the benchmark and Marcus will prepare the Console how-to.
13:12 Nina Patel: Thanks all — excited to see the benchmarks.
13:18 Liam Chen: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up.
